words.ex: Lack of sleep can affect your memory.
Music has a calming effect on babies.

mistakes.wrong: It has a big affect on me.
mistakes.right: It has a big effect on me.
mistakes.note: After a/the/big you need the noun effect.

groups.tip: Affect = Action (verb), Effect = End result (noun).

words.ex: She said that she was tired.

mistakes.wrong: He said me that…
mistakes.right: He told me that…
mistakes.note: A listener right after the verb → tell.

groups.tip: tell + person; say + words (or say to sb). Fixed: tell a story/the truth/a lie, say sorry.

words.ex: Can you make a cake for the party?
I need to do my homework.

mistakes.wrong: I made my homework.
mistakes.right: I did my homework.

mistakes.wrong: She did a mistake.
mistakes.right: She made a mistake.

groups.tip: make = create (a decision, a mistake, money, progress); do = activities (homework, research, your best).

words.ex: Could you lend me ten dollars?

mistakes.wrong: Can you borrow me your pen?
mistakes.right: Can you lend me your pen?
mistakes.note: You receive → borrow; you give → lend.

groups.tip: Borrow brings it to you (borrow from sb); lend sends it away (lend to sb).

words.ex: I'm going to lie down for a bit.
Please lay the papers on the desk.

mistakes.wrong: Yesterday I laid on the sofa all afternoon.
mistakes.right: Yesterday I lay on the sofa all afternoon.
mistakes.note: No object → lie – lay – lain; laid is the past of lay (put down).

groups.tip: Trap: the past of lie is lay. lie (tell a lie) – lied – lied.

words.ex: The sun rises in the east.

mistakes.wrong: The price of petrol has raised a lot.
mistakes.right: The price of petrol has risen a lot.

groups.tip: Raise always takes an object (raise something); rise never does: prices rise, a shop raises prices.

words.ex: Please bring your laptop when you come here.
Don't forget to take an umbrella when you go out.

mistakes.wrong: I'll bring the kids to school before I go to work.
mistakes.right: I'll take the kids to school before I go to work.
mistakes.note: Carrying away from where you are → take.

groups.tip: Bring = towards the speaker (here); take = away from the speaker (there).

words.def: look at something for a time
words.ex: We watched the match on TV.

mistakes.wrong: I like seeing football on TV.
mistakes.right: I like watching football on TV.
mistakes.note: Following something for a time → watch.

groups.tip: See just happens; look at is on purpose (often still things); watch is for a while, usually something moving (TV, a match).

mistakes.wrong: I listen music every day.
mistakes.right: I listen to music every day.

groups.tip: Hear just happens; listen is on purpose. With an object it is always listen to.

words.ex: We talked about our plans for hours.

mistakes.wrong: She can talk three languages.
mistakes.right: She can speak three languages.

groups.tip: Speak + a language (speak English) or formal speech; talk = have a conversation (talk to/with sb, about sth).

words.ex: I learnt to swim last summer.
She is studying medicine at university.

mistakes.wrong: I studied to ride a bike when I was six.
mistakes.right: I learned to ride a bike when I was six.
mistakes.note: Gaining a skill → learn to + verb.

groups.tip: Study is the effort (study for an exam); learn is the result – now you know it (learn to swim).

words.ex: Please remind me to call Mum.

mistakes.wrong: Remember me to call her.
mistakes.right: Remind me to call her.

groups.tip: Remind needs another person: remind sb to do / of sth; remember happens in your own head.

words.def: take from a person or place

mistakes.wrong: Someone robbed my phone on the bus.
mistakes.right: Someone stole my phone on the bus.
mistakes.note: The object is a thing → steal.

groups.tip: You rob a person or place (rob a bank); you steal a thing (steal a bike from sb).

mistakes.wrong: We won them.
mistakes.right: We beat them.
mistakes.note: win a game/prize; beat an opponent.

groups.tip: Win + a game, prize or medal; beat + the opponent.

mistakes.wrong: The trip was funny – we enjoyed every minute.
mistakes.right: The trip was fun – we enjoyed every minute.

groups.tip: Fun = enjoyable (a fun day); funny = makes you laugh (a funny joke).

words.ex: The country faces serious economic problems.
This car is very economical to run.

mistakes.wrong: This heater is very economic to run.
mistakes.right: This heater is very economical to run.

groups.tip: Economic = about the economy (economic growth); economical = saves money (an economical car).

mistakes.wrong: I enjoy historic films about ancient China.
mistakes.right: I enjoy historical films about ancient China.
mistakes.note: Set in the past (films, novels) → historical.

groups.tip: Historic = important in history (a historic day); historical = about the past (historical records).

mistakes.wrong: She plays classic music on the piano.
mistakes.right: She plays classical music on the piano.

groups.tip: Classical = the classical tradition or ancient Greece/Rome (classical music); classic = a top, typical example (a classic film, a classic mistake).

words.ex: She is very sensitive to criticism.

mistakes.wrong: My skin is very sensible to the sun.
mistakes.right: My skin is very sensitive to the sun.

groups.tip: Sensible = showing good sense (not 'sensitive'); sensitive = easily hurt or affected.

words.ex: This cake was made specially for you.

mistakes.wrong: I like sports, specially football.
mistakes.right: I like sports, especially football.

groups.tip: Especially = above all; specially = for one purpose (made specially for you).

mistakes.wrong: Beside, the hotel is close to the beach.
mistakes.right: Besides, the hotel is close to the beach.
mistakes.note: 'In addition' at the start of a sentence → Besides.

groups.tip: Beside = next to; add an s for 'in addition' → besides.

words.ex: The park is between the bank and the school.
The singer is popular among teenagers.

mistakes.wrong: The house is among the river and the forest.
mistakes.right: The house is between the river and the forest.

groups.tip: Between = separate, clear items (often two); among = inside a group or crowd.

words.ex: I've lived here for ten years.

mistakes.wrong: I have studied English since 5 years.
mistakes.right: I have studied English for 5 years.

groups.tip: For + a period (for three years); since + a starting point (since 2015, since Monday).

words.ex: I fell asleep during the film.

mistakes.wrong: I stayed in Da Nang during three days.
mistakes.right: I stayed in Da Nang for three days.

groups.tip: During + an event or period (when?); for + a length of time (how long?).

words.def: earlier than; at any time in the past
words.ex: I had met her two years before the wedding.

mistakes.wrong: I met him three years before, at university.
mistakes.right: I met him three years ago, at university.

groups.tip: Ago counts back from now, with the past simple (two days ago); before counts back from another past time (two days before the trip).

mistakes.wrong: I haven't already finished.
mistakes.right: I haven't finished yet.

groups.tip: Already = sooner than expected, in positive sentences, mid-sentence; yet = in negatives and questions, usually at the end.

mistakes.wrong: It's yet raining.
mistakes.right: It's still raining.

groups.tip: Still = something continues (before the main verb); yet in negatives = it hasn't happened (at the end).

words.ex: Every student in the school wears a uniform.
She had a bag in each hand.

mistakes.wrong: She wore a ring on every hand.
mistakes.right: She wore a ring on each hand.

groups.tip: Each = one by one, separately (works for two); every = all as a group (three or more). Both take a singular noun.

words.ex: I have a few friends here, so I'm not lonely.
Few people understood the lecture, so it was a failure.

mistakes.wrong: Don't worry, I have few friends here who can help.
mistakes.right: Don't worry, I have a few friends here who can help.

groups.tip: A few = some, enough (positive); few = almost none (negative). Both + plural countable nouns.

words.ex: There's a little milk left – enough for your tea.
There's little hope of finding them now.

mistakes.wrong: Hurry up! We have a little time left.
mistakes.right: Hurry up! We have little time left.

groups.tip: A little = some, enough (positive); little = almost none (negative). Both + uncountable nouns.

words.ex: There were fewer cars on the road.

mistakes.wrong: There were less people than last year.
mistakes.right: There were fewer people than last year.

groups.tip: Things you count (cars, people) → fewer; things you measure (sugar, time) → less.

words.ex: How many books do you have?
How much water do you drink?

mistakes.wrong: I don't have much friends.
mistakes.right: I don't have many friends.

groups.tip: Many + plural countable nouns; much + uncountable nouns. In positive sentences a lot of sounds more natural.

words.ex: He feels lonely in the big city.

mistakes.wrong: I like living lonely.
mistakes.right: I like living alone.

groups.tip: Alone = without other people (a fact); lonely = sad about it (a feeling). You can be alone without being lonely.

words.ex: I was bored during the lesson.

mistakes.wrong: I'm boring in this class.
mistakes.right: I'm bored in this class.

groups.tip: General rule: -ed = how you feel; -ing = what causes the feeling.

mistakes.wrong: I am interesting in music.
mistakes.right: I am interested in music.

groups.tip: -ed = how you feel (interested in); -ing = what makes you feel it (an interesting book).

words.ex: The children are excited about Tet.

mistakes.wrong: I'm so exciting about the trip.
mistakes.right: I'm so excited about the trip.

groups.tip: Excited = how a person feels (excited about); exciting = what causes it (an exciting trip).

words.ex: She got a new job at a bank.
I have a lot of work to do today.

mistakes.wrong: I'm looking for a work.
mistakes.right: I'm looking for a job. / I'm looking for work.
mistakes.note: work is uncountable – no a work.

groups.tip: Job is countable (a job, two jobs); work is uncountable and general (a lot of work, go to work).

words.ex: We went on a day trip to Ha Long.

words.def: the act of travelling from one place to another
words.ex: The journey from Hanoi to Hue takes 12 hours.

mistakes.wrong: I had a nice travel.
mistakes.right: I had a nice trip.
mistakes.note: travel as a noun is usually uncountable.

groups.tip: Travel = travelling in general (usually uncountable); trip = a visit there and back (a business trip); journey = getting from A to B.

words.def: an opinion about what to do
words.ex: Can you give me some advice?

mistakes.wrong: She gave me many advices.
mistakes.right: She gave me a lot of advice.

groups.tip: Advice (with c, said /s/) is the noun; advise (with s, said /z/) is the verb.

words.ex: You need to practise every day.

mistakes.wrong: We have football practise on Monday.
mistakes.right: We have football practice on Monday.
mistakes.note: The noun is always practice (UK and US).

groups.tip: American English uses practice for both.

mistakes.wrong: It's a matter of principal.
mistakes.right: It's a matter of principle.

groups.tip: The principal is your pal (head of a school; main); a principle is a rule (both end in -le).

words.ex: The wine is a perfect complement to the meal.

mistakes.wrong: She complemented me on my English.
mistakes.right: She complimented me on my English.

groups.tip: Compliment = praise (I like it!); complement = makes something complete.

words.ex: The traffic was stationary for an hour.

mistakes.wrong: I bought some stationary for school.
mistakes.right: I bought some stationery for school.

groups.tip: Stationary = standing still; stationery = envelopes, paper and pens.

mistakes.wrong: I don't want to loose my job.
mistakes.right: I don't want to lose my job.

groups.tip: Lose /luːz/ is the verb and has lost an o; loose /luːs/ is the adjective, with room for two.

mistakes.wrong: Please be quite in the library.
mistakes.right: Please be quiet in the library.

groups.tip: Quiet /ˈkwaɪət/ has two syllables = silent; quite /kwaɪt/ has one = fairly.

words.ex: We had lunch and then went shopping.

mistakes.wrong: My sister is older then me.
mistakes.right: My sister is older than me.

groups.tip: Than is for comparing; then is for when and next.

mistakes.wrong: The company changed it's name.
mistakes.right: The company changed its name.

groups.tip: Test: replace it with it is or it has. If that works, write it's; if not, write its (possessive, like his).

words.ex: The students left their bags here.

mistakes.wrong: Their are many problems.
mistakes.right: There are many problems.

groups.tip: Their contains heir (ownership); there contains here (place, there is); they're = they are.

mistakes.wrong: Who's bag is this?
mistakes.right: Whose bag is this?

groups.tip: Test: replace it with who is or who has. If that works, who's; if it means 'belonging to whom', whose.

mistakes.wrong: Your welcome!
mistakes.right: You're welcome!

groups.tip: Test: replace it with you are. If that works, you're; if not, your (belonging to you).

mistakes.wrong: I except your invitation.
mistakes.right: I accept your invitation.

groups.tip: Accept (verb) = take or agree to; except (preposition) = not including – ex- means 'out'.

words.ex: The school adopted a new policy.

mistakes.wrong: It took me months to adopt to life in London.
mistakes.right: It took me months to adapt to life in London.

groups.tip: Adapt = change to fit (adapt to); adopt = take as your own (adopt a child, adopt a policy).

words.def: leave your country to live elsewhere
words.ex: His family emigrated from Vietnam in 1990.

words.def: come into a country to live
words.ex: Many people immigrate to Canada every year.

mistakes.wrong: His family immigrated from Vietnam in 1990.
mistakes.right: His family emigrated from Vietnam in 1990.

groups.tip: Emigrate = exit your country (from); immigrate = come in to a new one (to). Same move, different point of view.

mistakes.wrong: The rain avoided us from going out.
mistakes.right: The rain prevented us from going out.

groups.tip: Prevent = stop something happening (prevent sb from doing); avoid = keep yourself away (avoid + -ing).

words.ex: These shoes don't fit me – they're too small.

mistakes.wrong: This dress doesn't suit me – it's too tight.
mistakes.right: This dress doesn't fit me – it's too tight.

groups.tip: Fit = the right size; suit = looks good on a person, or is convenient; match = two things go together.

words.ex: I expect it will rain later.
I'm looking forward to the holiday.

mistakes.wrong: I look forward to see you.
mistakes.right: I look forward to seeing you.

groups.tip: Expect = think it will happen; wait for = spend time until it happens; look forward to + -ing = feel happy about it.

words.ex: I hope you pass the exam.

mistakes.wrong: I wish you will pass the exam.
mistakes.right: I hope you pass the exam.

groups.tip: Hope = something possible (hope + present/future); wish = something unreal (wish + past: I wish I were…).

words.def: a good time to do something
words.ex: The job is a great opportunity to learn.
There is a possibility of rain.
Is there any chance you could help me?

mistakes.wrong: This job gives me the possibility to travel.
mistakes.right: This job gives me the opportunity to travel.
mistakes.note: A chance to do something → opportunity to.

groups.tip: Opportunity = a good moment to do something (to do); possibility = something might happen (of); chance can mean both and is less formal.

words.ex: The shop cut its prices for the sale.

words.def: money needed to do or get something
words.ex: The cost of living in cities is high.

mistakes.wrong: The price of living in Hanoi is rising.
mistakes.right: The cost of living in Hanoi is rising.
mistakes.note: Fixed phrase: the cost of living.

groups.tip: Price = what the seller asks; cost = what you must spend to do or get something (the cost of living).

words.ex: The minimum wage rose this year.

mistakes.wrong: The minimum salary rose this year.
mistakes.right: The minimum wage rose this year.

groups.tip: Salary = fixed monthly or yearly pay; wage = paid by the hour or week (the minimum wage).

words.ex: They bought a big house by the sea.

mistakes.wrong: I go to home after school.
mistakes.right: I go home after school.
mistakes.note: No to before home after verbs of movement.

groups.tip: House = the building; home = where you live and belong. go/come/get home – no to.

words.ex: Please ensure that all doors are locked.
I can assure you that it's safe.

mistakes.wrong: I ensure you that it's safe.
mistakes.right: I assure you that it's safe.

groups.tip: Ensure = make sure it happens; insure = buy insurance; assure = tell a person confidently (assure sb that…).

words.ex: She convinced me that she was right.

mistakes.wrong: He convinced that me to join.
mistakes.right: He persuaded me to join.

groups.tip: convince sb to V is common now; convince sb that is the core use.

mistakes.wrong: Who discovered the telephone?
mistakes.right: Who invented the telephone?

groups.tip: Discover = find something that already existed (a planet, a law of nature); invent = create something new (a machine).

words.ex: Sign your name at the end of the form.
In the end, we decided to stay.

mistakes.wrong: In the end of the film, they get married.
mistakes.right: At the end of the film, they get married.
mistakes.note: Followed by of → at the end of.

groups.tip: At the end of sth = the final point of it; in the end = finally, after everything (stands alone).

words.ex: We got to the cinema just in time to see the start.

mistakes.wrong: We arrived on time to catch the last bus.
mistakes.right: We arrived in time to catch the last bus.
mistakes.note: Early enough to do something → in time to.

groups.tip: On time = at the planned time; in time = early enough (in time for sth / to do).

mistakes.wrong: She works like a teacher.
mistakes.right: She works as a teacher.
mistakes.note: A real job or role → as.

groups.tip: Like = similar to (not really); as = in the role of (really).

mistakes.wrong: Let's have dinner together sometimes next week.
mistakes.right: Let's have dinner together sometime next week.

groups.tip: With -s = several times → sometimes; without → sometime (at some point).

words.ex: Smartphones are part of everyday life.

mistakes.wrong: I go jogging everyday.
mistakes.right: I go jogging every day.

groups.tip: Everyday (one word) is an adjective before a noun; every day = each day. If every single day works, write two words.

words.ex: The shop may be closed today.

mistakes.wrong: He maybe late today.
mistakes.right: He may be late today.
mistakes.note: The sentence needs a verb → may be.

groups.tip: Maybe (one word) = perhaps, usually at the start; may be is a verb – if might be works, write two words.

words.ex: The station is farther than I thought.

mistakes.wrong: The beach is more far than I thought.
mistakes.right: The beach is farther than I thought.

groups.tip: Physical distance: farther or further; 'more, additional' is only further (further information). Never more far.

words.ex: My brother is older than me.
My elder sister lives in Paris.

mistakes.wrong: My brother is two years elder than me.
mistakes.right: My brother is two years older than me.

groups.tip: Elder is for family members, before a noun (my elder sister); with than always use older.

words.ex: There was continuous rain for three days.
I'm tired of your continual complaints.

mistakes.wrong: We had continual rain for 48 hours without stopping.
mistakes.right: We had continuous rain for 48 hours without stopping.

groups.tip: Continuous = without a break (one unbroken line); continual = again and again, with breaks (often annoying).

words.ex: An efficient engine uses less fuel.

mistakes.wrong: This engine is very effective – it uses little fuel.
mistakes.right: This engine is very efficient – it uses little fuel.

groups.tip: Effective = gets the result you want; efficient = does it without wasting time, money or energy.

words.ex: Are you implying that I'm lying?
From his tone, I inferred that he was angry.

mistakes.wrong: Are you inferring that I'm lying?
mistakes.right: Are you implying that I'm lying?

groups.tip: The speaker implies; the listener infers. Meaning goes out of the speaker and into the listener.

mistakes.wrong: That will be 30 dollars all together.
mistakes.right: That will be 30 dollars altogether.

groups.tip: Altogether = in total; completely; all together = everyone at once (you can split it: we all went together).

words.ex: They sell live fish at the market.

mistakes.wrong: They sell alive crabs at the market.
mistakes.right: They sell live crabs at the market.

groups.tip: Alive goes after a verb (is alive); live /laɪv/ goes before a noun (live fish, live music).

words.ex: The storm caused serious damage to roads.

mistakes.wrong: The flood caused many damages.
mistakes.right: The flood caused a lot of damage.

groups.tip: Damage is mostly for things (buildings, roads); harm is mostly for people and health (there's no harm in…).

mistakes.wrong: Almost students like music.
mistakes.right: Most students like music. / Almost all students like music.
mistakes.note: almost can't go directly before a noun.

groups.tip: Almost = nearly, goes with all/every/no/always; most + noun = the majority (most students).

words.def: out of a hundred (with a number)

words.ex: The percentage of women in work increased.

mistakes.wrong: The percent of students who passed rose.
mistakes.right: The percentage of students who passed rose.

groups.tip: With a number → percent (20 percent); without a number → percentage (a high percentage of…).

mistakes.wrong: There are many peoples in the room.
mistakes.right: There are many people in the room.

groups.tip: Person = one; people = more than one and already plural (people are). Peoples means 'nations'.

mistakes.wrong: We must protect the nature.
mistakes.right: We must protect nature.

groups.tip: Nature (the natural world) takes no the; the environment always takes the.
